title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 2 - Numerical × Numerical
text:
A bit of math
As in Part 1, a model with an interaction between two predictors \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) looks like:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 (X_1 \times X_2) + \epsilon\]
The difference is that now both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are continuous. To see what the interaction coefficient \(\beta_3\) means here, we can rearrange the equation to group the terms involving \(X_1\):
\[Y = \beta_0 + (\beta_1 + \beta_3 X_2) X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \epsilon\]
The slope of \(X_1\) is no longer a single number: it is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 X_2\), a value that changes linearly with \(X_2\). For every one-unit increase in \(X_2\), the slope of \(X_1\) changes by \(\beta_3\). The same logic applies in the other direction: the slope of \(X_2\) is \(\beta_2 + \beta_3 X_1\). In Part 1, the interaction gave us one slope per group; here, we get a different slope for every value of the other predictor.
This also means that \(\beta_1\) alone is the slope of \(X_1\) only when \(X_2 = 0\) (and vice versa). Whether that value is meaningful depends on whether zero is a meaningful value of the other predictor, which is why centering predictors (more on this below) is often useful in models with numerical × numerical interactions.
For the simulated examples in this tutorial, we will be measuring the petal length of flowers in a forest. We are interested in the effect of environmental conditions on petal length.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 2 - Numerical × Numerical
text:
Simulating the dataset
Let’s simulate an initial dataset of 200 petal lengths, temperature and rain measurements.

n_flowers <- 200

temperature <- rnorm(n = n_flowers, mean = 10, sd = 15)

rain <- rgamma(n = n_flowers, shape = 2)

avg_petal_length <- 25.6

sd_petal_length <- 4.5

temperature_effect <- 0.4

rain_effect <- 0.9

interaction_effect <- 0.2

tibble(
  temp_centered = temperature - mean(temperature),
  rain_centered = rain - mean(rain),
  petal_length = rnorm(
    n = n_flowers,
    mean = avg_petal_length +
      temperature_effect * temp_centered +
      rain_effect * rain_centered +
      interaction_effect * temp_centered * rain_centered,
    sd = sd_petal_length
  )
) -> flower_measurements_1

You may notice in the code above that, in contrast to how we simulated Bighorn Sheep data in the first tutorial, we have centered the values of the predictors. In other words, we have subtracted the average temperature or rain value from the observations. This has for effect of shifting the model intercept. Rather than the intercept being the average petal length when rain and temperature = 0, it represents the average petal length for flowers exposed to average temperature and rain conditions. This makes its value (debatably) more pertinent to some research topics.

library(GGally)
ggpairs(
  flower_measurements_1,
  diag  = list(continuous = wrap("densityDiag", fill = "white", alpha = 0.6, color = "white")),
  lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", color = "white", alpha = 0.6, size = 2, shape = 1)),
  upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", color = "white", size = 5))
) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(color = "black", face = "bold", size = 12)
  )








Let’s fit a linear model to these data.

mod_flower_measurements_1 <- glmmTMB(petal_length ~ temp_centered * rain_centered, data = flower_measurements_1)

summary(mod_flower_measurements_1)

 Family: gaussian  ( identity )
Formula:          petal_length ~ temp_centered * rain_centered
Data: flower_measurements_1

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
   1170.4    1186.9    -580.2    1160.4       195 


Dispersion estimate for gaussian family (sigma^2): 19.4 

Conditional model:
                            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                 25.81489    0.31145   82.89  < 2e-16 ***
temp_centered                0.38644    0.02195   17.60  < 2e-16 ***
rain_centered                0.82921    0.21235    3.90 9.42e-05 ***
temp_centered:rain_centered  0.19534    0.01725   11.32  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


We can see from the model output that the model estimates our parameters pretty well.
Notice how we have gone straight to a model without having clearly defined our research questions. We now have a model output; every parameter has 3 stars which means we are significantly happy. But why? And, most importantly, what do these values mean?
Since our vague research objective is to quantify the effect of environmental conditions on petal length, let’s break down our model and extract as many effects as possible. This will help us understand interactions better and formulate more specific research questions.
Let us start with the Estimates for temp_centered and rain_centered. These are the slopes for temperature and rain when the other variable is set to zero. As we mean-centered these predictors, the estimates are the effect of one variable when the other is at its mean. Let’s validate this with the slopes() function.
Temperature effect when rain_centered = 0

slopes(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    rain_centered = 0
  ),
  variables = "temp_centered"
)


 rain_centered Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
             0    0.386      0.022 17.6   <0.001 228.0 0.343  0.429

Term: temp_centered
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX


Rain effect when temperature_centered = 0

slopes(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    temp_centered = 0
  ),
  variables = "rain_centered"
)


 temp_centered Estimate Std. Error   z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
             0    0.829      0.212 3.9   <0.001 13.4 0.413   1.25

Term: rain_centered
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX


However, these are the effect of one predictor when the other is set to a single value. As we specified an interaction in the model, we may be more interested in the slope of one of the variables across the range of the values of the other. We will add the average back to the centered values to get the raw values of the predictors back.
Effect of rain:

slopes_by_temp <- slopes(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    temp_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        max(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        length.out = 30
    )
  ),
  variables = "rain_centered",
  by = "temp_centered"
)

trend_slope_temp <- coef(lm(estimate ~ temp_centered, data = slopes_by_temp))[["temp_centered"]]

slopes_by_temp |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = temp_centered + mean(temperature), ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    alpha = 0.4,
    fill = "lightgrey"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = temp_centered + mean(temperature), y = estimate),
    lineend = "round",
    linewidth = 2,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = -Inf, y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.2, vjust = 1.5,
    label = paste0("slope = ", round(trend_slope_temp, 3)),
    color = "white", size = 6, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-25, 50, by = 5)) +
  labs(
    y = "Effect of rain on petal length",
    x = "Temperature values"
  )








We can see that rain has a negative effect on petal length when temperatures are below 5.
Effect of temperature:

slopes_by_rain <- slopes(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(rain_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                                         max(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                                         length.out = 30
  )),
  variables = "temp_centered",
  by = "rain_centered"
)

trend_slope <- coef(lm(estimate ~ rain_centered, data = slopes_by_rain))[["rain_centered"]]

slopes_by_rain |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = rain_centered + mean(rain), ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
    alpha = 0.4,
    fill = "lightgrey"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = rain_centered + mean(rain), y = estimate),
    lineend = "round",
    linewidth = 2,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = -Inf, y = Inf,
    hjust = -0.2, vjust = 1.5,
    label = paste0("slope = ", round(trend_slope, 3)),
    color = "white", size = 6, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  labs(
    y = "Effect of temperature on petal length",
    x = "Rain values"
  )








Temperature has a positive effect for all values of rain but that effect increases as rain increases.
We can obtain similar plots using the plot_slopes() function.
The slope obtained between the effect of one predictor and the values of the other is the interaction parameter we obtain in the model output. This is the moderating effect that the predictors have on one another. As we did not have a very specific research question, we can report both of the plots above as a description of how temperature and rain moderate each other’s effect on petal length. In many contexts, however, we have apriori hypotheses about how variables interact within a system. For example, if we study a drought-resistant plant, we may hypothesize that temperature (the exposure variable) is the most relevant factor that could affect petal length (the outcome) but its effect is moderated by rain (the moderator). If that is the case, let’s look at some ways to display the model predictions.
We can start by looking at the predicted average petal length as a function of temperature for different values of rain. The choice of moderator values for which we generate predictions can vary depending on the research question. It is common to choose certain quantiles of the moderator. In this example, we will use the five-number summary for rain values.

predictions(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    temp_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        max(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        length.out = 30
    ),
    rain_centered = fivenum
  )
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rain = round(rain_centered + mean(rain), 2)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(y = estimate,
                x = temp_centered + mean(temperature),
                color = as.factor(rain)),
            lineend = "round",
            linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low,
                  ymax = conf.high,
                  x = temp_centered + mean(temperature),
                  fill = as.factor(rain)),
              alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    y = "Predicted petal length",
    x = "Temperature",
    color = "Rain",
    fill = "Rain"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50))

mutate: new variable 'rain' (double) with 5 unique values and 0% NA









If we ignore the fact that the model predicts negative petal lengths when temperature is low and rain is high (7.79), visualizing the model predictions this way clearly shows how the effect of temperature on petal length varies with/is moderated by rain values.
Another way to visualize these trends is to generate a response surface.

predictions(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    temp_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        max(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        length.out = 30
    ),
    rain_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                        max(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                        length.out = 30
    )
  )
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rain = rain_centered + mean(rain),
         temp = temp_centered + mean(temperature)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rain, y = temp, z = estimate)) +
  stat_contour_filled() +
  labs(
    y = "Temperature",
    x = "Rain",
    fill = "Predicted petal length"
  )

mutate: new variable 'rain' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'temp' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA









The advantage of these plots is that we can see how the predictions change for all combinations of the exposure (temperature) and moderator (rain). For example, if we focus on rain = 6 and look up from the bottom of the y-axis to the top (as temperature increases), we can see the predicted petal length increase substantially (again, ignoring the fact that negative values are predicted). I personally prefer plots such as the one with predictions for the five-number summary as they are less of a mind-bender and it is easier to see the uncertainty related to the predicted mean. I’ve also noticed that response surfaces displayed as such lead people to over-interpretation of the results. As we can arbitrarily change the values in each color bin (yellow could be for predicted petal lengths of 60-90 instead of 80-90), and the 95% confidence intervals are missing, we can overemphasize effects that, in reality, are poorly supported by the model.
For fun, let’s visualize this response surface in 3D with the 95% confidence intervals. I would not necessarily recommend these plots for a publication but they can be a useful way to better understand the model predictions and their uncertainty. These plots will also be informative for future topics in this tutorial series.

library(ggcube)

predictions(mod_flower_measurements_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    temp_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        max(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                        length.out = 30
    ),
    rain_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                        max(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                        length.out = 30
    )
  )
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    rain = rain_centered + mean(rain),
    temp = temp_centered + mean(temperature)
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  stat_surface_3d(aes(x = rain, y = temp, z = conf.high), fill = "red", alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_surface_3d(aes(x = rain, y = temp, z = estimate), fill = "blue") +
  stat_surface_3d(aes(x = rain, y = temp, z = conf.low), fill = "red", alpha = 0.4) +
  coord_3d(light = "none") +
  labs(
    z = "Petal length",
    x = "Rain",
    y = "Temp"
  ) -> resp_surface_3d

animate_3d(resp_surface_3d, yaw = c(0, 360))








The animation does not render the way I would like it to but I hope the reader can still appreciate the shape of the response surface in all its dimensions. We will explore response surfaces of different shapes in a future tutorial on interactions with Generalized Additive Models (GAMs).

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 2 - Numerical × Numerical
text:
What we learned

Numerical × numerical interactions mean variable-dependent slopes: With an interaction, the slope of one predictor changes linearly with the value of the other. The interaction coefficient \(\beta_3\) is the amount by which the slope of one predictor changes for a one-unit increase in the other.
Centering helps interpretation: When predictors are mean-centered, the “main effect” coefficients are the slopes of each predictor when the other is at its average, and the intercept is the predicted response under average conditions.
Plot the slopes, not just the coefficients: Plotting the slope of one predictor across the range of the other (with slopes()) shows where an effect is positive, negative, or indistinguishable from zero.
Choose visualizations for your question: Conditional prediction lines at chosen moderator values (e.g., the five-number summary) are usually easier to interpret than response surfaces, which lack uncertainty information and can encourage over-interpretation.
Interactions are not only for the mean: With distributional regression (e.g., dispformula in glmmTMB), predictors can interact in their effect on the standard deviation of the response. Visualizing the full predicted distributions (with the distributional and ggdist packages) helps interpret how the modeled parameters act together.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 2 - Numerical × Numerical
text:
Tools for interpretation

slopes() with by =: Get the slope of one predictor across values of the other
predictions() with datagrid(): Generate conditional predictions at chosen combinations of predictor values (e.g., fivenum for the moderator)
type = "disp": Get predictions or slopes for the dispersion (standard deviation) model
plot_slopes() and plot_predictions(): Quick versions of the plots we built manually

In the next part of this series, we will look at interactions in generalized linear models, where non-linear link functions add another layer of complexity to interpretation.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
text:
In this third part of my tutorial series on statistical interactions, we are going to push further on our understanding and reporting of interactions. Since we are going beyond the realm of linear models by exploring generalized linear models (GLMs) and their variants, I am assuming here that the reader has a basic understanding of how GLMs work especially concerning their use of link functions.
I typically write up these tutorials based on bits and pieces of information I have gathered here and there but I will (in part) address topics covered specifically by Spake et al. (2023) https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/brv.12939 and Mize (2019) https://sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/ while giving examples of tools that can be used to report interaction effects on the additive and multiplicative scale.
The case studies in this tutorial will focus on species occurence and abundance. We will first look at habitat suitability for a given species to occur in a given location. Second, we will explore factors that affect their abundance when they are present. Third, we will incorporate both these processes in a single model and learn how to extract as much information as possible from these types of analyses.


First, we load the relevant packages and set up our ggplot2 theme for the rest of the document.

# Load the packages used throughout (install any you are missing first)
library(tidyverse)       # Data manipulation and plotting
library(tidylog)         # Print a log of data manipulations done with tidyverse
library(glmmTMB)         # Generalized linear (mixed) models
library(marginaleffects) # Compute marginal/conditional effects
library(patchwork)       # Combine multiple plots
library(distributional)  # Simulate distributions
library(ggdist)          # Plot nice distributions
library(GGally)          # ggpairs(): scatterplot matrix of all variables
library(tinytable)       # tt(): simple, nice-looking results tables
library(performance)     # r2(), r2_tjur(): model R-squared measures


# Set ggplot2 theme
black_theme <- theme(
  axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 2, lineend = "round", color = "white"),
  panel.grid = element_blank(),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
  axis.ticks = element_blank(),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold", color = "white"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold", color = "white"),
  plot.title = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold", color = "white"),
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 21, color = "white"),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold", color = "white"),
  legend.position = "bottom"
)

theme_set(black_theme)

# Set global default for geom_point shape
update_geom_defaults("point", list(shape = 1, size = 3, alpha = 0.8))

# silence marginaleffects warnings about glmmTMB
options(marginaleffects_safe = FALSE)

# Fix the random number generator so the simulated data are reproducible
set.seed(333)

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: The interaction on the count scale
text:
The interaction on the count scale
On the count scale, we can ask: how does the slope of scl_prey (in individuals per SD of prey abundance) change across different levels of scl_competitors? If there were no interaction, this slope would be flat across competitor levels — any curvature here reflects the explicit interaction we built in, layered on top of the implicit curvature the log link always contributes.

# Slope of scl_prey on the response scale across 30 values of scaled competitors
# (for a hurdle model, glmmTMB's "response" combines occupancy and abundance-when-present)
slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey",
       newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30)),
       type = "response") |> as_tibble() -> slopes_prey_by_comp_response

ggplot(slopes_prey_by_comp_response) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = scl_competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = scl_competitors, y = estimate), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round", color = "white") +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(count scale, individuals present)", x = "Competitors (scaled)",
       title = "Count-scale effect of prey availability weakens as competitors increase")








The slope of prey availability on abundance (when present) starts out detectably positive at low competitor density and shrinks toward (and across) zero as competitor density increases — consistent with the simulated story that competitors suppress the per-capita benefit of extra prey.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: The interaction on the rate-ratio scale
text:
The interaction on the rate-ratio scale
The count-scale picture above mixes together the explicit prey * competitors interaction and the implicit curvature from exponentiating the linear predictor (the same \[\lambda \cdot \beta\] logic from Case Study 2). To isolate something closer to “the interaction itself,” we move to the rate-ratio scale: for each one-SD increase in competitors, by what factor does the effect of one extra SD of prey get multiplied? That’s exp() of the interaction coefficient, and because it lives on the model’s own additive (log) scale, it doesn’t depend on where competitors are evaluated — unlike the count-scale slope above.

# Goal: rate ratio of scl_prey (exp of the log-scale slope) at competitors = -1, 0, +1 SD
rate_ratio_interaction_tbl <- avg_slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey",
                                          by = "scl_competitors",
                                          newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = c(-1, 0, 1)),
                                          type = "link") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = exp(estimate), rr_low = exp(conf.low), rr_high = exp(conf.high)) |>
  select(scl_competitors, rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high, p.value) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    p.value = if_else(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(p.value, 3)))
  ) |>
  mutate(CI_95 = glue::glue("[{rr_low}, {rr_high}]")) |>
  select(`Competitors (scaled)` = scl_competitors, `Rate ratio for scl_prey` = rate_ratio, `95% CI` = CI_95, `p-value` = p.value)

Reading this table: at low competitor density (-1 SD), a one-SD increase in prey is associated with a modest increase in expected abundance (rate ratio ≈ 1.08). At average competitor density (0 SD), that same one-SD increase in prey comes with a rate ratio just under 1 (≈ 0.91) — essentially no effect. By the time competitors reach +1 SD, the rate ratio has fallen to about 0.76: a one-SD increase in prey is now associated with fewer individuals, not more. The ratio of these rate ratios, comparing low to high competitor density, is exactly exp(-0.176 * 2), the exponentiated interaction coefficient scaled to a two-SD contrast in competitors — a single number that, unlike the count-scale slopes above, is constant no matter what scl_prey itself is held at.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: Slope-by-predictor plots: link vs. response scale
text:
Slope-by-predictor plots: link vs. response scale
Finally, let’s put the link-scale and response-scale views of this interaction side by side, the same way we did for mod_1’s implicit interaction in Case Study 1. Here the link-scale panel should not be flat, because scl_prey:scl_competitors is an explicit term in the conditional formula — any curvature we see in the response-scale panel is a mix of that explicit interaction and the implicit curvature from the log link, whereas the link-scale panel isolates the explicit interaction alone.

# Same slopes on the link (log) scale: the explicit interaction shows as a straight-line trend
slopes_prey_by_comp_link <- slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey",
  newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30)),
  type = "link"
) |> as_tibble()

p_comp_response <- slopes_prey_by_comp_response |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = scl_competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = scl_competitors, y = estimate), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round", color = "white") +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(count scale)", x = "Competitors (scaled)", title = "Response scale")

p_comp_link <- slopes_prey_by_comp_link |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = scl_competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = scl_competitors, y = estimate), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round", color = "white") +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(log scale)", x = "Competitors (scaled)", title = "Link scale")

p_comp_response + p_comp_link








On the link (log) scale, the slope of scl_prey declines in a straight line as competitors increase — that’s the explicit interaction term, additive by construction on the scale the model was fit on. On the response (count) scale, the same decline is visible but curved and compressed toward zero at high competitor density, because low abundance plots have little room left for the slope to move on the count scale (the \[\lambda \cdot \beta\] logic again, now layered on top of an already-declining \[\beta\]). Both panels tell a consistent story — prey only helps when competitors are scarce — but only the link-scale panel isolates that story from the implicit curvature every log-link model carries, which is why the rate-ratio table above is often the cleaner number to report alongside a plot like this one. When we look at the y-axis of the previous plots, the values there are standardized coefficients. These represent the degree to which the count or log(count) change with a one-standard deviation increase in the predictors. However, the x-axis also shows the scaled values of the moderating variable (competitors) which is hard to interpret. We might prefer showing the raw values of competitors instead.

# Same plots as before, but unscale_x() converts the x-axis back to raw competitor counts
p_comp_response_raw <- slopes_prey_by_comp_response |>
  mutate(competitors = unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round", color = "white") +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(count scale)", x = "Competitors", title = "Response scale")

mutate: new variable 'competitors' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

p_comp_link_raw <- slopes_prey_by_comp_link |>
  mutate(competitors = unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round", color = "white") +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(log scale)", x = "Competitors", title = "Link scale")

mutate: new variable 'competitors' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

p_comp_response_raw + p_comp_link_raw








With unscale_x() reversing the standardization, the x-axis now reads in the original units of competitor abundance (individuals), while the y-axis stays on the standardized-prey slope scale from before — the shape of each curve is identical to the scaled version, just relabeled onto a scale that’s easier to communicate.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: Predicted abundance across prey and competitors, at five-number-summary values
text:
Predicted abundance across prey and competitors, at five-number-summary values
So far we’ve only ever looked at the interaction through its slope — how steeply abundance changes with prey at a given competitor level. It’s worth also looking directly at the predicted trends themselves, the way we did for the numerical × numerical case in an earlier tutorial: plot predicted abundance against prey, with one line per competitor level, choosing those competitor levels from the moderator’s five-number summary (fivenum()) rather than an arbitrary round number. As before, unscale_x() converts both axes back to their natural, more interpretable units.

# Conditional (abundance-when-present) predictions on a prey grid, one line per competitor
# five-number-summary value; unscale_x() maps back to natural units for plotting
predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(
    scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
    scl_competitors = fivenum
  ),
  type = "conditional"
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(prey = unscale_x(pop_data$prey, scl_prey),
         competitors = round(unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors), 1)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = as.factor(competitors)), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate, color = as.factor(competitors)), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Prey", color = "Competitors", fill = "Competitors")

mutate: new variable 'prey' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'competitors' (double) with 5 unique values and 0% NA









These are type = "conditional" predictions — abundance in plots where the species is already present, exactly like the “when present” curve from the simple hurdle example earlier in this case study. At the lowest observed competitor count (0), predicted abundance climbs steeply and fairly uncertainly as prey increases; by the time competitors reach their 75th-percentile value, the prey curve is nearly flat, mirroring the shrinking count-scale slope we saw above.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: The population-scale picture: prey × competitors at low vs. high tree cover
text:
The population-scale picture: prey × competitors at low vs. high tree cover
The conditional predictions above only describe abundance given occupancy — they say nothing about whether a plot is occupied in the first place, which is exactly what scl_tree_cov governs in the zero-inflation part of mod_hu. To get the full population-scale picture (type = "response"), we need to also account for tree cover. Just like we did for mod_2 in Case Study 2, we can exploit the fact that tree_cov is bimodal and evaluate predictions separately at its two density peaks, so that “low tree cover” and “high tree cover” plots are each represented by a value that’s actually common in the simulated data, rather than an arbitrary round number.

# Locate the two peaks of tree_cov's bimodal distribution, as scaled values
# (mod_hu's zero-inflation formula uses scl_tree_cov, not tree_cov)
d <- density(pop_data$tree_cov)
peaks <- d$x[which(diff(sign(diff(d$y))) == -2) + 1]
low_tree <- round(peaks[1], 2)
high_tree <- round(peaks[length(peaks)], 2)
low_tree_scl <- scale_x(pop_data$tree_cov)[which.min(abs(pop_data$tree_cov - low_tree))]
high_tree_scl <- scale_x(pop_data$tree_cov)[which.min(abs(pop_data$tree_cov - high_tree))]

# Population-scale ("response") predictions: prey grid x competitor quintiles x tree-cover peaks
predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(
    scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
    scl_competitors = fivenum,
    scl_tree_cov = c(low_tree_scl, high_tree_scl)
  ),
  type = "response"
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(prey = unscale_x(pop_data$prey, scl_prey),
         competitors = round(unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors), 1),
         `Tree cover` = if_else(scl_tree_cov == low_tree_scl, "Low tree cover", "High tree cover")) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = as.factor(competitors)), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate, color = as.factor(competitors)), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  facet_wrap(~ `Tree cover`) +
  labs(y = "Predicted population abundance", x = "Prey", color = "Competitors", fill = "Competitors")

mutate: new variable 'prey' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'competitors' (double) with 5 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'Tree cover' (character) with 2 unique values and 0% NA









Two things stand out here. First, within each panel, the prey × competitors interaction looks qualitatively the same as it did on the conditional scale above: a steep, uncertain climb with prey when competitors are scarce, flattening out as competitors increase. That’s expected, since population-scale abundance is just conditional abundance scaled down by occupancy probability, and occupancy doesn’t depend on prey or competitors in this model. Second, and more informative, the two panels show overall lower predicted population abundance at low tree cover than at high tree cover, even though the shapes of the curves within each panel are similar — because fewer plots are occupied at all when tree cover is low, pulling every curve down by roughly the same multiplicative factor. In other words, tree cover and the prey × competitors interaction act on largely separate parts of this model: tree cover mostly shifts how many plots have the species at all, while prey and competitors jointly shape abundance within the plots where it does.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: A symmetric interaction, viewed from the other predictor
text:
A symmetric interaction, viewed from the other predictor
Spake et al. (2023) make a point that’s easy to lose sight of once a plot like the one above has become the “default” way of showing an interaction: a two-way interaction term is, mathematically, perfectly symmetric. scl_prey:scl_competitors is the exact same coefficient as scl_competitors:scl_prey — there is no sense in which the model treats prey as “the” focal variable and competitors as “the” moderator, or vice versa. That choice is entirely ours, made for narrative convenience (we picked prey as the x-axis because the conservation question was framed around “how much does prey availability help”), not because the statistics privilege one direction over the other. Spake et al. flag this as a common source of asymmetric or incomplete interaction reporting: papers will show (and discuss at length) the effect of A moderated by B, but never show the mathematically identical effect of B moderated by A, even though the two views can highlight different, equally valid practical takeaways.
Here, showing the interaction the other way around — competitors on the x-axis, with one line per level of prey’s five-number summary — makes a point that’s much harder to see in the prey-on-the-x-axis version: regardless of how much prey is available, a sufficiently high density of competitors drives expected abundance down to roughly the same low floor. The lines, which fan out dramatically at low competitor density (echoing the steep low-competitor slopes we found earlier), converge almost on top of each other once competitors exceed about 4–5 individuals.

# Same idea with axes swapped: competitors on x, one line per prey five-number-summary value
# (conditional = abundance when present)
predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(
    scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
    scl_prey = fivenum
  ),
  type = "conditional"
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(competitors = unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors),
         prey = round(unscale_x(pop_data$prey, scl_prey), 1)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = as.factor(prey)), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate, color = as.factor(prey)), linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Competitors", color = "Prey", fill = "Prey")

mutate: new variable 'competitors' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'prey' (double) with 5 unique values and 0% NA









Both this plot and the prey-on-the-x-axis version a few sections back are legitimate, complete descriptions of the exact same fitted interaction — neither one is “more correct.” But they emphasize different conservation-relevant messages: the prey-focused framing emphasizes that boosting prey only helps when competitors are already scarce, while the competitor-focused framing emphasizes that reducing competitors is what reliably moves abundance, almost regardless of how much prey is available. Reporting only one direction, as Spake et al. caution, risks leaving a reader with just half of a symmetric effect.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: Average predictions: collapsing the interaction into one curve per predictor
text:
Average predictions: collapsing the interaction into one curve per predictor
Everything up to this point has described the interaction conditionally — the effect of prey at a specific level of competitors, or vice versa. Sometimes we instead want a single summary curve per predictor that integrates over the other predictor’s (and tree cover’s) observed distribution, the same “average effect” idea from avg_predictions()/avg_slopes() that we used for mod_1 back in Case Study 1 — there, a one-line call like avg_predictions(mod_1, variables = "tree_cov") was all we needed. Here, we instead build the grid explicitly with datagrid(..., grid_type = "counterfactual") before handing it to avg_predictions(..., by = "scl_prey"). Why the extra step, and is it actually doing something different?
It’s worth checking directly, because the two approaches can look deceptively similar. avg_predictions(variables = "focal") is really shorthand: internally, it builds a grid that crosses the requested sequence of the focal variable against every observed row of the data — exactly a counterfactual grid — and then averages the resulting predictions within each focal value. That’s a different (and, for our purposes, more correct) procedure than simply calling datagrid(focal = seq(...)) by itself, which instead holds every other predictor fixed at a single representative value (the mean, for numeric predictors) and gives you the prediction at that one point, not an average over the sample. We can see the gap between these two directly using mod_1, which has no explicit interaction:

# avg_predictions(variables = "tree_cov"), the shorthand we used in Case Study 1
# Counterfactual grid: each focal value is paired with EVERY observed row of the data,
# so predictions are averaged over the real distribution of the other predictors.
# 1) the shorthand used in Case Study 1
shorthand_avg <- avg_predictions(mod_1, variables = "tree_cov", type = "response") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(tree_cov, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

select: dropped 5 variables (std.error, statistic, p.value, s.value, df)

# The same thing, spelled out explicitly with grid_type = "counterfactual"
counterfactual_avg <- avg_predictions(mod_1,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_1, tree_cov = sort(unique(shorthand_avg$tree_cov)), grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "tree_cov", type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |> select(tree_cov, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

select: dropped 5 variables (std.error, statistic, p.value, s.value, df)

# Contrast: a *plain* datagrid(), which holds rain and temp at their mean instead of averaging over them
mean_held_avg <- avg_predictions(mod_1,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_1, tree_cov = sort(unique(shorthand_avg$tree_cov))),
  by = "tree_cov", type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |> select(tree_cov, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

select: dropped 5 variables (std.error, statistic, p.value, s.value, df)

The first two tables are identical: avg_predictions(variables = "tree_cov") and the explicit counterfactual-grid version are computing exactly the same thing, confirming that variables = "focal" was already doing counterfactual averaging under the hood all along. The third table, built from a plain datagrid() that holds rain and temp at their means, is close but not identical — here the discrepancy is small because mod_1 has no interaction, so the slope of tree_cov barely changes across the range of rain and temp (the “implicit interaction” from Case Study 1 is weak for this particular predictor pair).
So why spell out grid_type = "counterfactual" explicitly for mod_hu instead of using the variables = "focal" shorthand, if the two are the same? Purely a practical reason: the shorthand’s automatic sequence of focal values is a fixed default (a short grid of representative points), whereas we wanted a smooth 30-point sequence spanning the full observed range of prey and competitors for plotting, and datagrid() is how you specify that. The averaging is identical either way — for a model without any explicit interaction (like mod_1), the choice barely matters in practice, but for mod_hu, where prey’s effect on abundance genuinely depends on competitor density, it matters more that the average is a true average over the observed joint distribution of competitors and tree cover, not a slope evaluated at their means.

When present (conditional scale)

# Average prey curve (abundance when present): averaged over all observed competitors and tree cover
avg_pred_prey_cond <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_prey", type = "conditional"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(prey = unscale_x(pop_data$prey, scl_prey))

mutate: new variable 'prey' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

# Same for competitors, averaged over observed prey
avg_pred_comp_cond <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_competitors", type = "conditional"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(competitors = unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors))

mutate: new variable 'competitors' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

p_avg_prey_cond <- avg_pred_prey_cond |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "white", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Prey")

p_avg_comp_cond <- avg_pred_comp_cond |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "white", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Competitors")

p_avg_prey_cond + p_avg_comp_cond








Averaged over the full range of competitors actually observed, prey still shows a positive, accelerating relationship with abundance (when present) — unsurprising, since we saw above that prey only loses its positive effect once competitors get reasonably dense, and most simulated plots have more modest competitor counts. Competitors, averaged over the full observed range of prey, show a steep decline that flattens out: a textbook diminishing-returns (or diminishing-harm) shape once competitor density is already high.


Population-wide (response scale), at low vs. high tree cover
The same averaging logic applies on the population scale, where we again take advantage of tree_cov’s two density peaks to compare “low tree cover” and “high tree cover” populations directly, each curve now representing the average effect of prey (or competitors) across the full observed range of the other predictor.

# Population-scale average curves, kept separate for the two tree-cover peaks
# (response = occupancy x abundance when present)
avg_pred_prey_resp <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
                      scl_tree_cov = c(low_tree_scl, high_tree_scl),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = c("scl_prey", "scl_tree_cov"), type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(prey = unscale_x(pop_data$prey, scl_prey),
         `Tree cover` = if_else(scl_tree_cov == low_tree_scl, "Low tree cover", "High tree cover"))

mutate: new variable 'prey' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'Tree cover' (character) with 2 unique values and 0% NA

avg_pred_comp_resp <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
                      scl_tree_cov = c(low_tree_scl, high_tree_scl),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = c("scl_competitors", "scl_tree_cov"), type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(competitors = unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors),
         `Tree cover` = if_else(scl_tree_cov == low_tree_scl, "Low tree cover", "High tree cover"))

mutate: new variable 'competitors' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'Tree cover' (character) with 2 unique values and 0% NA

p_avg_prey_resp <- avg_pred_prey_resp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prey, y = estimate, color = `Tree cover`, fill = `Tree cover`)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted\npopulation abundance", x = "Prey")

p_avg_comp_resp <- avg_pred_comp_resp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate, color = `Tree cover`, fill = `Tree cover`)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted\npopulation abundance", x = "Competitors")

p_avg_prey_resp + p_avg_comp_resp








As in the fivenum-by-tree-cover plot earlier, the shapes of the prey and competitors curves are essentially unchanged between the two tree-cover panels — the interaction with prey/competitors lives entirely in the conditional (truncated-Poisson) part of the model, which doesn’t know anything about tree cover. What does change is the overall height of the curves: high-tree-cover populations sit consistently above low-tree-cover ones, because more plots are occupied in the first place when tree cover is high. The gap between the two Tree cover lines is therefore a pure occupancy effect, while the shape of each individual line is a pure abundance-when-present effect — a nice visual confirmation that this hurdle model keeps the two processes cleanly separated.


Average effect for the population, across all tree cover values
Finally, if we don’t want to split by tree cover at all — for instance, because our research question is about the overall population response rather than a tree-cover-specific one — we can let grid_type = "counterfactual" integrate over the full observed distribution of tree_cov as well, giving one population-scale curve per predictor that already reflects the mix of low- and high-tree-cover plots actually present in the data.

# Population-scale average curves, averaging over ALL observed tree cover values too
avg_pred_prey_resp_all <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_prey", type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(prey = unscale_x(pop_data$prey, scl_prey))

mutate: new variable 'prey' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

avg_pred_comp_resp_all <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_competitors", type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(competitors = unscale_x(pop_data$competitors, scl_competitors))

mutate: new variable 'competitors' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

p_avg_prey_resp_all <- avg_pred_prey_resp_all |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "white", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted population\nabundance (all tree cover)", x = "Prey")

p_avg_comp_resp_all <- avg_pred_comp_resp_all |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "white", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted population\nabundance (all tree cover)", x = "Competitors")

p_avg_prey_resp_all + p_avg_comp_resp_all








These two curves are what we’d report if a reviewer asked for “the” effect of prey or competitors on population abundance, without reference to tree cover at all: each one is a single number (or curve) that already has tree cover’s bimodal distribution baked in, roughly splitting the difference between the low- and high-tree-cover curves from the previous plot, weighted by how common each kind of plot actually is in the simulated sample. Compared to the “when present” curves above, both are compressed toward zero and flatter in absolute terms, since every point on these curves also carries the (roughly 14%) chance that the plot isn’t occupied at all.
We can apply the exact same counterfactual-averaging logic to tree cover itself, this time integrating over the full observed distribution of prey and competitors instead of holding them fixed.

# Average population-scale prediction across tree cover (affects only the zero-inflation part)
avg_pred_tree_resp_all <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_tree_cov = seq(min(pop_data$scl_tree_cov), max(pop_data$scl_tree_cov), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_tree_cov", type = "response"
) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(tree_cov = unscale_x(pop_data$tree_cov, scl_tree_cov))

mutate: new variable 'tree_cov' (double) with 30 unique values and 0% NA

avg_pred_tree_resp_all |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = tree_cov, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "white", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = tree_cov, y = estimate), color = "white", linewidth = 1.5, lineend = "round") +
  labs(y = "Average predicted population\nabundance", x = "Tree cover")








Unlike the prey and competitors curves above, this one isn’t flattened by averaging over an interaction — tree cover doesn’t interact with anything in mod_hu, it only ever appears in the zero-inflation formula. The steady, roughly linear rise here is therefore a clean population-scale read-out of tree cover’s effect on occupancy alone: going from no tree cover to full tree cover is associated with expected population abundance increasing from about 0.23 to 0.37 individuals per plot, averaged over the full observed range of prey and competitor abundance. That’s a useful contrast with the prey and competitors curves just above — this one shows what it looks like to average over an interaction-free predictor, where there’s no risk of the averaging masking different effects at different levels of some other variable.
This is A LOT of figures and information. And we have not even plotted these effects on the rate-ratio scale or log-odds scale. What should we report in our publication? This all depends on the research question. If we want to make recommendations about how we can better conserve our species by acting on either of the three variables we focused on, we could report the figures we have generated above which relate more to raw abundance increase. To answer questions relating to how these variables affect population dynamics (on a rate scale), we could report these in the form of a table as these rates are assumed to be linear in these models and are thus easier to interpret in a table form compared to potentially non-linear relationships on the probability and count scales.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
section: A full rate-ratio results table, by model component
text:
A full rate-ratio results table, by model component
Let’s build that table, following the same approach as mod2_tbl in Case Study 2: pull every fixed-effect slope on the link scale and exponentiate it into a rate ratio, keeping coefficients standardized throughout so they’re directly comparable to one another. mod_hu has two components — the conditional (truncated-Poisson) part describing abundance when present, and the zero-inflation (binomial) part describing occupancy — so we report rate ratios separately for each, with a clear label for which component (and, where relevant, which moderator value) each row describes.
For scl_tree_cov in the zero-inflation part, a quick note on interpretation: glmmTMB’s zero-inflation formula models the probability of a structural zero (the plot being unsuitable/unoccupied), not the probability of occurrence directly. So exp() of that coefficient is an odds ratio for becoming a structural zero, not a rate ratio for abundance — a rate ratio below 1 here means higher tree cover is associated with lower odds of the plot being a structural zero, i.e. higher occupancy, consistent with how we simulated the data.
Because scl_prey and scl_competitors interact, neither has a single rate ratio that applies everywhere — exactly the implicit-interaction-on-top-of-explicit-interaction idea from earlier in this case study. So, following the same scheme we used for temp’s effect at low vs. high tree cover back in Case Study 2, we report each one’s rate ratio at three representative levels of the other (-1 SD, 0 SD, +1 SD), plus the interaction term itself — the ratio of these rate ratios per 1-SD increase in the moderator — as a single row that doesn’t depend on where the other predictor is evaluated.

# Goal: one rate-ratio table for mod_hu, with a Component column for each model part.
# avg_slopes(type = "link") gives log-scale slopes; exp() converts them to rate ratios.
# Conditional-model rate ratio for scl_prey, at three levels of scl_competitors
prey_rr_tbl <- avg_slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey", by = "scl_competitors",
                           newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = c(-1, 0, 1)),
                           type = "link") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = exp(estimate), rr_low = exp(conf.low), rr_high = exp(conf.high),
         Term = glue::glue("scl_prey (at scl_competitors = {scl_competitors} SD)")) |>
  select(Term, rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high, p.value)

mutate: new variable 'rate_ratio' (double) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'rr_low' (double) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'rr_high' (double) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'Term' (character) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
select: dropped 9 variables (term, contrast, scl_competitors, estimate, std.error, …)

# Conditional-model rate ratio for scl_competitors, at three levels of scl_prey
comp_rr_tbl <- avg_slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_competitors", by = "scl_prey",
                           newdata = datagrid(scl_prey = c(-1, 0, 1)),
                           type = "link") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = exp(estimate), rr_low = exp(conf.low), rr_high = exp(conf.high),
         Term = glue::glue("scl_competitors (at scl_prey = {scl_prey} SD)")) |>
  select(Term, rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high, p.value)

mutate: new variable 'rate_ratio' (double) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'rr_low' (double) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'rr_high' (double) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
        new variable 'Term' (character) with 3 unique values and 0% NA
select: dropped 9 variables (term, contrast, scl_prey, estimate, std.error, …)

# The interaction itself: ratio of rate ratios per 1-SD increase in the moderator,
# constant regardless of where the other predictor is evaluated
hu_confint <- confint(mod_hu)
hu_coef_cond <- summary(mod_hu)$coefficients$cond
hu_coef_zi <- summary(mod_hu)$coefficients$zi

interaction_rr_tbl <- tibble(
  Term = "scl_prey:scl_competitors (interaction)",
  rate_ratio = exp(hu_coef_cond["scl_prey:scl_competitors", "Estimate"]),
  rr_low = exp(hu_confint["cond.scl_prey:scl_competitors", "2.5 %"]),
  rr_high = exp(hu_confint["cond.scl_prey:scl_competitors", "97.5 %"]),
  p.value = hu_coef_cond["scl_prey:scl_competitors", "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

# Zero-inflation-model odds ratio for scl_tree_cov (no moderator: tree cover
# doesn't interact with anything in this model)
zi_rr_tbl <- tibble(
  Term = "scl_tree_cov (zero-inflation)",
  rate_ratio = exp(hu_coef_zi["scl_tree_cov", "Estimate"]),
  rr_low = exp(hu_confint["zi.scl_tree_cov", "2.5 %"]),
  rr_high = exp(hu_confint["zi.scl_tree_cov", "97.5 %"]),
  p.value = hu_coef_zi["scl_tree_cov", "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

# Combine the four pieces, round, format CIs, and keep a tidy set of columns
hu_rr_tbl <- bind_rows(
  prey_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Conditional (abundance, when present)"),
  comp_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Conditional (abundance, when present)"),
  interaction_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Conditional (abundance, when present)"),
  zi_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Zero-inflation (occupancy, as an odds ratio)")
) |>

  mutate(

Reading this table component by component: in the conditional (abundance-when-present) part, scl_prey‘s rate ratio shrinks from about 1.24 at low competitor density down to about 0.81 at high competitor density — crossing 1 somewhere around average competitor density, which is why its “main effect” row back in summary(mod_hu) looked like noise (estimate ≈ 0, p ≈ 0.95). scl_competitors’s rate ratio is below 1 at every level of prey we checked, but gets progressively further from 1 (stronger suppression) as prey increases — competitors matter more when there’s more prey worth competing over. The interaction row (≈0.81, CI excluding 1) is the single number behind both of those patterns: for every 1-SD increase in competitors, prey’s rate ratio gets multiplied by about 0.81 (and symmetrically, for every 1-SD increase in prey, competitors’ rate ratio gets multiplied by the same 0.81 — the symmetry point from earlier in this case study, right there in the table). In the zero-inflation part, scl_tree_cov’s odds ratio (≈0.82, CI excluding 1) tells a simpler, interaction-free story: each 1-SD increase in tree cover is associated with about an 18% reduction in the odds that a plot is a structural zero, i.e., higher occupancy — consistent with the steady rise we saw in the population-scale tree-cover prediction curve above.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
text:
What we learned

Link functions create implicit interactions: Even without an explicit interaction term, a non-linear link function (logit, log, …) makes every predictor’s effect on the response scale depend on the values of all the other predictors. This is purely a consequence of the curvature of the link, not evidence of a “real” interaction in the data-generating process.
The scale you report on changes what you see: On the link scale, effects are additive and (without an explicit interaction term) perfectly flat across the other predictors. On the response scale, the same model can show a strongly curving, moderator-dependent effect. Whether an interaction “exists” can depend entirely on which scale you ask the question on (Spake et al.’s additive vs. multiplicative distinction).
Local slopes vs. scale-invariant ratios: A response-scale slope (e.g., individuals per unit of a predictor, or probability points per unit) only applies at the specific covariate values it was evaluated at. A rate ratio \[e^\beta\] odds ratio, etc. on the link scale is constant everywhere on the curve, which makes it a natural summary number when you want one value per predictor that doesn’t depend on where the other predictors are set — at the cost of being harder to translate into a concrete “how many individuals” statement.
Interactions are symmetric: A two-way interaction term describes a single, mathematically symmetric relationship between two predictors. Showing only “A moderated by B” and never “B moderated by A” risks reporting just half of the story, even though both views are equally valid and can emphasize different practical conclusions.
Hurdle and zero-inflated models split a response into separate processes: A hurdle model lets us interpret the occurrence (binomial) and abundance-when-present (truncated count) parts separately, each with its own predictors and link function, or combine them into a single population-scale prediction (occurrence probability × conditional abundance). Both views are useful, depending on whether the research question is about presence, abundance given presence, or abundance across the whole landscape.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models: Part 3 - Generalized Linear Models
text:
Tools for interpretation

slopes() / avg_slopes() with type = "response" vs. type = "link": Compare a predictor’s effect on the natural (probability, count) scale against its effect on the scale the model is additive on.
predictions() / avg_predictions() with type = "conditional", "response", or "zprob": For hurdle/zero-inflated models, get predictions from just the count part, the full population-scale combination, or the probability of a structural zero.
datagrid(..., grid_type = "counterfactual"): Average predictions or slopes over the observed distribution of the other predictors, rather than holding them at a single representative value (e.g., their mean).
Exponentiating link-scale slopes (exp(estimate)): Turn a log-odds or log-count coefficient into an odds ratio or rate ratio that stays constant regardless of where the other predictors are evaluated.
fivenum() and density peaks (density()): Choose informative, data-driven values of a moderator (e.g., for faceting or line colors) instead of arbitrary round numbers, especially for bimodal predictors like tree cover in this tutorial.

In the next part of this series, we will look at interactions in generalized additive models (GAMs), where the response surface can bend in ways that a linear or polynomial interaction term cannot capture.

# Installation des packages nécessaires (exécuter seulement si besoin)

title: ENT101: Échantillonnage du campus UdS
text:
2.2 Introduction au tidyverse
Le tidyverse est une collection cohérente de packages R conçus pour la science des données. Il révolutionne la façon dont nous travaillons avec les données en R en offrant une syntaxe claire, lisible et cohérente.

2.2.1 Principes fondamentaux du tidyverse
Le tidyverse repose sur la philosophie des “tidy data” (données bien organisées) :

Chaque variable forme une colonne : Une seule variable par colonne
Chaque observation forme une ligne : Une seule observation par ligne

Chaque valeur a sa propre cellule : Une seule valeur par cellule
Un type d’unité d’observation par tableau : Ne pas mélanger différents types de données


2.2.1.1 L’opérateur pipe (|>)
L’opérateur pipe (|>) est l’un des outils les plus puissants du tidyverse. Il permet de :
Principe de base :
# Au lieu d'écrire : fonction2(fonction1(donnees, argument1), argument2)
# On peut écrire : donnees |> fonction1(argument1) |> fonction2(argument2)
Exemple concret :

# Méthode traditionnelle (difficile à lire)
# resultat <- filter(select(mutate(pieges, nouveau = ancienne * 2), nouveau, site), site == 1)

# Méthode avec pipe (facile à lire et comprendre)
# resultat <- pieges |>
#   mutate(nouveau = ancienne * 2) |>
#   select(nouveau, site) |>
#   filter(site == 1)



2.2.1.2 Avantages du pipe

Lisibilité améliorée : Le code se lit de gauche à droite, comme une phrase
Moins d’objets intermédiaires : Évite de créer des variables temporaires
Débogage facilité : On peut exécuter le code ligne par ligne
Logique claire : Chaque étape de transformation est explicite



2.2.1.3 Packages principaux du tidyverse utilisés dans ce tutoriel

dplyr : Manipulation de données (filter, select, mutate, summarise)
ggplot2 : Création de graphiques élégants
tidyr : Restructuration des données (pivot_longer, pivot_wider)
readr : Lecture de fichiers de données
purrr : Programmation fonctionnelle
stringr : Manipulation de chaînes de caractères



2.2.1.4 Exemple pratique de workflow tidyverse

# Exemple typique d'un workflow tidyverse (sera détaillé plus tard)
# donnees |>                           # Prendre les données
#   filter(condition) |>               # Filtrer selon une condition
#   mutate(nouvelle_variable = ...) |> # Créer une nouvelle variable
#   group_by(groupe) |>                # Grouper par une variable
#   summarise(moyenne = mean(...)) |>  # Calculer des statistiques
#   ggplot(aes(x = ..., y = ...)) +    # Créer un graphique
#   geom_point()                       # Ajouter des points

Pourquoi adopter cette approche ? - Efficacité : Moins de code, plus de clarté - Reproductibilité : Code plus facile à comprendre et à maintenir - Apprentissage : Syntaxe cohérente entre tous les packages - Collaboration : Standard adopté par la communauté R
Cette philosophie sera omniprésente dans tout le tutoriel. Chaque manipulation de données utilisera cette approche pour maximiser la clarté et la reproductibilité du code.



2.2.2 Avantages de travailler avec des documents Quarto/R Markdown
Ce tutoriel utilise le format Quarto (extension .qmd), une évolution moderne de R Markdown. Ces formats offrent de nombreux avantages pour l’analyse de données scientifiques :

2.2.2.1 Recherche reproductible
Intégration code-texte : - Code et explications ensemble : Le code, les résultats et les explications sont dans le même document - Exécution automatique : Les graphiques et tableaux sont générés automatiquement à partir du code - Pas de copier-coller : Élimination des erreurs de transfert manuel entre logiciels


2.2.2.2 Documentation vivante
Mise à jour automatique : - Résultats toujours à jour : Quand les données changent, tout le document se met à jour - Traçabilité complète : Chaque résultat peut être retracé jusqu’au code qui l’a généré - Versions cohérentes : Impossible d’avoir des résultats qui ne correspondent pas au code


2.2.2.3 Flexibilité de sortie
Formats multiples : - HTML : Pour la visualisation interactive et le partage web - PDF : Pour les rapports formels et publications - Word : Pour la collaboration avec des collègues non-techniques - Présentations : Slides directement à partir du même code


2.2.2.4 Avantages pédagogiques
Apprentissage structuré : - Progression logique : Code et explications s’enchaînent naturellement - Contexte immédiat : Chaque bout de code est expliqué dans son contexte - Expérimentation facile : Modifier le code et voir immédiatement les résultats


2.2.2.5 Collaboration scientifique
Partage efficace : - Tout inclus : Un seul fichier contient analyse, méthodes et résultats - Contrôle de version : Compatible avec Git pour le travail d’équipe - Transparence : Les méthodes sont explicites et vérifiables


2.2.2.6 Exemple pratique

# Ce bloc de code sera exécuté et ses résultats affichés automatiquement
# Exemple simple pour démontrer l'intégration
exemple_donnees <- data.frame(
  x = 1:5,
  y = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
)

# Le graphique apparaîtra directement dans le document final
# ggplot(exemple_donnees, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
#   geom_point() +
#   labs(title = "Exemple d'intégration code-résultats")

Pourquoi c’est révolutionnaire : - Fin des “ça marchait sur mon ordinateur” : L’environnement est documenté - Science ouverte : Méthodes complètement transparentes et reproductibles - Gain de temps : Plus besoin de refaire manuellement les graphiques après modifications - Qualité : Moins d’erreurs, plus de cohérence
Ce format est devenu la norme en science des données et recherche reproductible. Vous constaterez ces avantages tout au long de ce tutoriel !

title: ENT101: Échantillonnage du campus UdS
section: 2.3 Gestion des projets R et bonnes pratiques de reproductibilité
text:
2.3 Gestion des projets R et bonnes pratiques de reproductibilité

2.3.1 Importance des projets R (R Projects)
Avant de commencer l’analyse, il est crucial de comprendre l’importance d’organiser son travail dans un projet R. Un projet R crée un environnement de travail isolé et portable qui facilite la collaboration et la reproductibilité.

2.3.1.1 Problèmes avec setwd() et chemins absolus
❌ Mauvaise pratique :
# Ne jamais faire cela !
setwd("/Users/MonNom/Documents/projet_entomo/")
donnees <- read_csv("donnees/mes_donnees.csv")
Problèmes causés par setwd() :

Non-reproductible : Le chemin /Users/MonNom/Documents/ n’existe que sur un ordinateur spécifique
Fragile : Si le dossier est déplacé, le code ne fonctionne plus
Collaboration impossible : Vos collègues ne peuvent pas exécuter votre code
Maintenance difficile : Difficile de réorganiser les fichiers
Erreurs fréquentes : Changements de répertoire non intentionnels



2.3.1.2 Solutions avec les projets R
✅ Bonne pratique :
# Avec un projet R, tous les chemins sont relatifs
donnees <- read_csv("donnees/mes_donnees.csv")
# ou
donnees <- read_csv(here::here("donnees", "mes_donnees.csv"))
Avantages des projets R :

Reproductibilité : Le code fonctionne sur n’importe quel ordinateur
Portabilité : Facile de déplacer ou partager tout le projet
Organisation : Structure claire et logique des fichiers
Collaboration : Plusieurs personnes peuvent travailler sur le même projet
Versionning : Compatible avec Git pour le contrôle de version



2.3.1.3 Structure recommandée d’un projet d’entomologie
projet_entomo/
├── projet_entomo.Rproj        # Fichier de projet R
├── README.md                  # Documentation du projet
├── donnees/                   # Données brutes (ne jamais modifier)
│   ├── spatiales/
│   │   ├── pieges.gpkg
│   │   └── sites.gpkg
│   └── biologiques/
│       └── captures.xlsx
├── donnees_traitees/          # Données nettoyées/transformées
├── scripts/                   # Scripts R d'analyse
│   ├── 01_nettoyage.R
│   ├── 02_analyses.R
│   └── 03_visualisations.R
├── graphiques/                # Graphiques exportés
├── rapports/                  # Rapports et documents
└── fonctions/                 # Fonctions personnalisées


2.3.1.4 Le package here pour les chemins
Le package here résout élégamment les problèmes de chemins :
# Installation et chargement
install.packages("here")
library(here)

# Utilisation
donnees <- read_csv(here("donnees", "spatiales", "pieges.gpkg"))
ggsave(here("graphiques", "carte_sites.png"), plot = ma_carte)
Avantages de here() : - Trouve automatiquement la racine du projet - Fonctionne sur tous les systèmes d’exploitation - Chemins toujours relatifs au projet - Compatible avec RStudio et autres IDE



2.3.2 Workflow reproductible recommandé

Créer un nouveau projet R dans RStudio
Organiser les dossiers selon la structure recommandée
Utiliser des chemins relatifs avec here()
Documenter le projet avec un README.md
Versionner avec Git pour suivre les modifications
Tester la reproductibilité sur un autre ordinateur



2.3.3 Exemple pratique pour ce tutoriel
# Ce tutoriel assume que vous travaillez dans un projet R
# Tous les chemins seront relatifs, comme :
pieges <- st_read(here("donnees", "spatiales", "pieges.gpkg"))
captures <- read_xlsx(here("donnees", "biologiques", "captures.xlsx"))

# Au lieu de chemins absolus problématiques :
# pieges <- st_read("/Users/MonNom/projet/donnees/spatiales/pieges.gpkg")
Message important : Si vous voyez setwd() dans du code R, considérez-le comme un signal d’alarme pour les problèmes de reproductibilité. Préférez toujours l’approche par projets R !

title: ENT101: Échantillonnage du campus UdS
section: 3.1 Introduction à ggplot2 et personnalisation des graphiques
text:
3.1 Introduction à ggplot2 et personnalisation des graphiques

3.1.1 La grammaire des graphiques avec ggplot2
ggplot2 est l’un des packages les plus puissants et populaires de R pour la création de visualisations. Il est basé sur la “Grammar of Graphics”, une approche systématique pour construire des graphiques par couches.

3.1.1.1 Anatomie d’un graphique ggplot2
# Structure de base d'un graphique ggplot2
ggplot(data = mes_donnees, aes(x = variable_x, y = variable_y)) +
  geom_point() +                    # Couche géométrique (points)
  scale_x_continuous() +            # Échelle pour l'axe X
  scale_y_continuous() +            # Échelle pour l'axe Y
  labs(title = "Mon titre") +       # Étiquettes
  theme_minimal()                   # Thème graphique
Composants principaux : 1. Données (data) : Le jeu de données à visualiser 2. Esthétiques (aes) : Mapping des variables aux propriétés visuelles 3. Géométries (geom_*) : Type de représentation (points, lignes, barres, etc.) 4. Échelles (scale_*) : Contrôle des axes et légendes 5. Étiquettes (labs) : Titres, sous-titres, légendes 6. Thèmes (theme_*) : Apparence générale du graphique



3.1.2 Thèmes ggplot2 : De la base à la personnalisation
Les thèmes contrôlent l’apparence non-liée aux données de vos graphiques. ggplot2 offre plusieurs thèmes pré-formatés ainsi que des options de personnalisation complète.

3.1.2.1 Thèmes pré-formatés utilisés dans ce tutoriel


3.1.2.2 Démonstration des différents thèmes


[1] "1. Thème par défaut (theme_gray)"



graphique_base










[1] "2. theme_minimal() - Épuré et moderne"



graphique_base + theme_minimal()










[1] "3. theme_classic() - Style traditionnel"



graphique_base + theme_classic()










[1] "4. theme_bw() - Fond blanc avec bordures"



graphique_base + theme_bw()










[1] "5. theme_void() - Minimaliste absolu"



graphique_base + theme_void()










3.1.2.3 Thèmes recommandés pour la recherche scientifique
Pour les publications scientifiques : - theme_classic() : Apparence traditionnelle, axes sans grille - theme_bw() : Fond blanc, grilles discrètes - theme_minimal() : Moderne et épuré (utilisé dans ce tutoriel)
Pour les présentations : - theme_minimal() : Lisible et moderne - theme_void() : Pour les cartes et diagrammes simples


3.1.2.4 Personnalisation avancée des thèmes
Vous pouvez modifier n’importe quel élément d’un thème avec theme() :

# Exemple de personnalisation complète
graphique_personnalise <- graphique_base +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    # Titre principal
    plot.title = element_text(
      size = 16, 
      face = "bold", 
      hjust = 0.5,
      color = "darkblue"
    ),
    # Axes
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),

Ressources pour aller plus loin : - Documentation officielle : ?theme - Galerie ggplot2 : https://r-graph-gallery.com/ - Extension ggthemes : thèmes additionnels professionnels


3.1.4 Sauvegarde des graphiques avec ggsave()
La fonction ggsave() est l’outil standard pour exporter vos graphiques dans différents formats.

3.1.4.1 Syntaxe de base

# Créer un graphique
mon_graphique <- ggplot(donnees_exemple, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Mon graphique à sauvegarder")

# Sauvegarder le graphique
ggsave(
  filename = "mon_graphique.png",  # Nom du fichier
  plot = mon_graphique,            # Objet graphique (optionnel si dernier plot)
  width = 8,                       # Largeur en pouces
  height = 6,                      # Hauteur en pouces
  dpi = 300                        # Résolution (300 DPI pour publication)
)



[1] "Graphique sauvegardé dans mon_graphique.png"




3.1.4.2 Formats de sortie supportés

# PNG - Idéal pour le web et présentations
ggsave("graphique.png", mon_graphique, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

# PDF - Vectoriel, parfait pour les publications
ggsave("graphique.pdf", mon_graphique, width = 8, height = 6)

# SVG - Vectoriel, modifiable dans Illustrator
ggsave("graphique.svg", mon_graphique, width = 8, height = 6)

# TIFF - Format courant en recherche
ggsave("graphique.tiff", mon_graphique, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

# JPEG - Plus compressé que PNG
ggsave("graphique.jpg", mon_graphique, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300, quality = 95)



3.1.4.3 Conseils pour la sauvegarde
Résolutions recommandées : - 72-150 DPI : Web, présentations PowerPoint - 300 DPI : Publications scientifiques, rapports imprimés - 600 DPI : Impression haute qualité
Formats recommandés selon l’usage : - PNG : Graphiques avec transparence, usage général - PDF : Publications scientifiques (vectoriel, redimensionnable) - SVG : Retouches graphiques ultérieures - TIFF : Certaines revues scientifiques l’exigent
Dimensions typiques :
# Figure simple
ggsave("figure.png", width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)

# Figure large (deux colonnes)
ggsave("figure_large.png", width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)

# Figure carrée (pour certains graphiques)
ggsave("figure_carree.png", width = 6, height = 6, dpi = 300)


3.1.4.4 Intégration avec les projets R
# Avec le package here pour chemins relatifs
library(here)

# Sauvegarder dans le dossier graphiques du projet
ggsave(
  here("graphiques", "analyse_captures.png"),

  width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300
)
Astuce : Créez toujours vos graphiques avec des dimensions et résolutions adaptées à leur utilisation finale !
