                  scl_competitors (at scl_prey = -1 SD)
                  0.650
                  [0.565, 0.748]
                  <0.001
                
                
                  Conditional (abundance, when present)
                  scl_competitors (at scl_prey = 0 SD)
                  0.505
                  [0.456, 0.559]
                  <0.001
                
                
                  Conditional (abundance, when present)
                  scl_competitors (at scl_prey = 1 SD)
                  0.392
                  [0.341, 0.45]
                  <0.001
                
                
                  Conditional (abundance, when present)
                  scl_prey:scl_competitors (interaction)
                  0.776
                  [0.705, 0.855]
                  <0.001
                
                
                  Zero-inflation (occupancy, as an odds ratio)
                  scl_tree_cov (zero-inflation)
                  0.898
                  [0.81, 0.996]
                  0.041
                
        
      
    



Prey’s rate ratio crosses 1 somewhere around average competitor density (why its raw summary() estimate looked like noise); competitors suppress abundance more as prey increases; the interaction row (~0.81) is the single number behind both patterns, and it’s the same number whichever predictor you treat as the moderator — the symmetry point from a few slides back, visible directly in the table. Tree cover’s odds ratio in the zero-inflation part tells a simpler, interaction-free story about occupancy alone.

title: Understanding Interactions in Regression Models
text:
Exercise 7 / Homework
Now apply what we learned today to your data!

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
What is an interaction?
An interaction means the effect of one predictor depends on the value of another.

No interaction: snow depth affects weight the same way for every sheep
Interaction: the effect of snow depth on weight differs by sex

For a categorical moderator (e.g., sex) and a continuous predictor (e.g., snow depth): the interaction means the slope differs between categories.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Conditional vs. marginal effects

Conditional effects: the effect of a predictor at specific values of other predictors (e.g., the slope of snow depth for males)
Marginal effects: the effect averaged across the distribution of other predictors (e.g., the average slope of snow depth across the whole population)

Both are legitimate; they answer different questions. Interactions are exactly where the distinction starts to matter.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Why? Sex is a confounder

Within each sex: more snow → lower weight (true negative relationship)
Between sexes: males see more snow and are heavier (confounded)
Pooled data compares heavy, high-snow males to light, low-snow females → spurious positive trend


ggplot(bighorn_population) +
  geom_point(aes(x = snow_depth, y = weight, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = snow_depth, y = weight), method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = snow_depth, y = weight, color = sex), method = "lm", se = FALSE)




Within-sex trends are negative, as expected.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Marginal vs conditional, visualized

avg_pred_mass_1 <- avg_predictions(mod_mass_1, variables = "snow_depth")
pred_sex_mass_1 <- predictions(mod_mass_1, newdata = bighorn_mass_1)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = avg_pred_mass_1,
              aes(x = snow_depth, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
              color = "lightgreen", fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = avg_pred_mass_1, aes(x = snow_depth, y = estimate),
            color = "lightgreen") +
  geom_ribbon(data = pred_sex_mass_1,
              aes(x = snow_depth, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, color = sex, fill = sex),
              alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = pred_sex_mass_1, aes(x = snow_depth, y = estimate, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(data = bighorn_mass_1, aes(y = weight, x = snow_depth, color = sex)) +
  guides(alpha = "none", fill = "none") +
  labs(title = "Green = marginal; red/blue = conditional (by sex)") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(50, 220))




Green = marginal; red/blue = conditional (by sex).

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Part 1 takeaways

Interactions → conditional effects that depend on other variables
Simpson’s Paradox is a real risk when pooling across confounded groups
Marginal ≠ conditional; both are valid but answer different questions
Raw model coefficients rarely equal your research quantity of interest — use marginaleffects
Marginal effects inherit your sample’s covariate distribution unless you override it with newdata

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Two numerical predictors
With two continuous predictors, an interaction means: the slope of one predictor changes as the other predictor changes — not a separate slope per group, but a sliding one.
A raw coefficient is only “the slope when the other predictor equals zero” — meaningful only if zero is a meaningful value. This motivates centering predictors on their mean, so the intercept and main-effect coefficients describe average conditions.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Response surfaces — use with caution

predictions(mod_flower_1,
  newdata = datagrid(
    temp_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered),
                         max(flower_measurements_1$temp_centered), length.out = 30),
    rain_centered = seq(min(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered),
                         max(flower_measurements_1$rain_centered), length.out = 30)
  )) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rain = rain_centered + mean(rain), temp = temp_centered + mean(temperature)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rain, y = temp, z = estimate)) +
  stat_contour_filled() +
  labs(x = "Rain", y = "Temperature", fill = "Predicted petal length")








Contour bins are arbitrary and hide uncertainty — good for exploration, risky for publication-quality inference. Prefer line-and-ribbon plots when you can.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Checking the dispersion model

pred_sd_temp <- predictions(mod_flower_2, newdata = flower_measurements_2, type = "disp") |>
  as_tibble()

true_sd_temp <- flower_measurements_2 |>
  mutate(true_sd = exp(log_sd_intercept + log_sd_temp_slope * temp_centered))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = true_sd_temp,
            aes(x = temp_centered + mean(temperature), y = true_sd, color = "Simulated"),
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(data = pred_sd_temp,
              aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, x = temp_centered + mean(temperature)),
              fill = "red", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = pred_sd_temp,
            aes(x = temp_centered + mean(temperature), y = estimate, color = "Estimated")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Simulated" = "darkgreen", "Estimated" = "red"), name = "Standard deviation") +
  labs(x = "Temperature", y = "Standard deviation")




Recovered vs. simulated standard deviation of petal length.




type = "disp" retrieves predictions/slopes for the dispersion sub-model, exactly as type = "conditional" does for the mean.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: Simulating and fitting interactions on the standard deviation
text:
Simulating and fitting interactions on the standard deviation

log_sd_rain_slope <- 0.02
log_sd_interaction_effect <- 0.005

flower_measurements_3 <- tibble(
  temp_centered = temperature - mean(temperature),
  rain_centered = rain - mean(rain),
  petal_length = rnorm(
    n = n_flowers,
    mean = avg_petal_length +
      temperature_effect * temp_centered +
      rain_effect * rain_centered,
    sd = exp(log_sd_intercept +
      log_sd_temp_slope * temp_centered +
      log_sd_rain_slope * rain_centered +
      log_sd_interaction_effect * temp_centered * rain_centered))
)

mod_flower_measurements_3 <- glmmTMB(petal_length ~ temp_centered + rain_centered,
                                     dispformula = ~ temp_centered + rain_centered + temp_centered * rain_centered,
                                     data = flower_measurements_3)

We can interpret the interactive effects of rain and temperature on the standard deviation of petal length in the same way that we would for the average (see the Numerical x Numerical Interactions tutorial for worked examples). Another way to communicate the results: since the two parameters of the Normal distribution act together to generate the observations, we can predict new distributions of observations for different predictor values.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Part 2 takeaways

With two numerical predictors, the interaction coefficient is the rate of change of one slope per unit of the other — not a separate slope for each group
Centering predictors makes main-effect coefficients interpretable as “effect at average conditions”
Plot slopes across the moderator’s range, not just the coefficient table
Five-number-summary prediction plots are usually more honest than response surfaces (they retain uncertainty)
Interactions can act on variance, not just the mean, via distributional regression (dispformula)

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Fit the model

mod_1 <- glmmTMB(occurence ~ tree_cov + rain + temp, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = occ_data)
summary(mod_1)$coefficients$cond

               Estimate Std. Error    z value     Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -1.69327695 0.50024494 -3.3848957 7.120530e-04
tree_cov     1.98151874 0.43421560  4.5634443 5.032116e-06
rain        -0.02254920 0.06512181 -0.3462619 7.291459e-01
temp         0.04989717 0.01677791  2.9739804 2.939638e-03
attr(,"ddf")
[1] "asymptotic"


We simulated the effect of tree cover to be 0.45 on the probability scale, but the model reports ~1.87. That’s not an error — it’s reporting the coefficient on the log-odds scale, not the probability scale.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
marginaleffects does this for us

slopes(mod_1, variables = "tree_cov",
       newdata = datagrid(temp = mean(occ_data$temp), rain = mean(occ_data$rain)))


 temp rain Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 % 97.5 %
 19.5 4.22    0.491      0.107 4.57   <0.001 17.6  0.28  0.702

Term: tree_cov
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX


slopes() in this case asks: “at these covariate values, how much does predicted probability change for a small increase in tree cover?” — a probability-scale answer, directly comparable to how we simulated the data.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: Response vs. link scale, across each moderator
text:
Response vs. link scale, across each moderator

slopes_by_temp_response <- slopes(mod_1,
  newdata = datagrid(temp = seq(min(occ_data$temp), max(occ_data$temp), length.out = 30),
                      rain = mean(occ_data$rain)),
  variables = "tree_cov", by = "temp", type = "response") |> as_tibble()

slopes_by_temp_link <- slopes(mod_1,
  newdata = datagrid(temp = seq(min(occ_data$temp), max(occ_data$temp), length.out = 30),
                      rain = mean(occ_data$rain)),
  variables = "tree_cov", by = "temp", type = "link") |> as_tibble()

slopes_by_rain_response <- slopes(mod_1,
  newdata = datagrid(rain = seq(min(occ_data$rain), max(occ_data$rain), length.out = 30),
                      temp = mean(occ_data$temp)),
  variables = "tree_cov", by = "rain", type = "response") |> as_tibble()

slopes_by_rain_link <- slopes(mod_1,
  newdata = datagrid(rain = seq(min(occ_data$rain), max(occ_data$rain), length.out = 30),
                      temp = mean(occ_data$temp)),
  variables = "tree_cov", by = "rain", type = "link") |> as_tibble()

plot_slope <- function(data, x, y_lab, scale_title) {
  ggplot(data) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 2) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(x = .data[[x]], ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
    geom_line(aes(x = .data[[x]], y = estimate)) +
    labs(y = y_lab, x = x, title = scale_title)
}

(plot_slope(slopes_by_temp_response, "temp", "Slope of tree_cov\n(probability scale)", "Response scale") +
 plot_slope(slopes_by_temp_link, "temp", "Slope of tree_cov\n(log-odds scale)", "Link scale")) /
(plot_slope(slopes_by_rain_response, "rain", "Slope of tree_cov\n(probability scale)", "Response scale") +
 plot_slope(slopes_by_rain_link, "rain", "Slope of tree_cov\n(log-odds scale)", "Link scale"))




Slope of tree_cov across temp (top) and rain (bottom), on the probability (left) vs. log-odds (right) scale.




Link (log-odds) scale: the slope of tree_cov is flat (~1.87) across both moderators — exactly as it should be, since mod_1’s formula has no interaction term at all. Response (probability) scale: the slope visibly curves with temp (and more weakly with rain) — the implicit interaction made concrete, purely from the logit link’s curvature. With three predictors, a focal variable’s slope can no longer be shown across “the” moderator in one 2D plot — each panel above holds the other remaining predictor fixed at its mean. Alternatives: facet by the third variable, use small multiples at representative (e.g. five-number-summary) values, or report a single avg_slopes() that integrates over the observed distribution instead of fixing it.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
The “overall” effect of tree cover

avg_predictions(mod_1, variables = "tree_cov", vcov = TRUE) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = tree_cov, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(x = tree_cov, y = estimate)) +
  labs(y = "Predicted occurence")




Predicted probability of occurrence across tree_cov, averaged over the observed rain and temp values (counterfactual averaging).




avg_predictions()/avg_slopes() give one number (or curve) per focal value, integrating over rain and temp as observed in the sample — a marginal, “average effect” alternative to picking a single moderator value to condition on.

text:
Reviewer 2 wants a table

# Average slopes on the probability scale for all three predictors
slopes_tbl_mod1 <- avg_slopes(mod_1, variables = c("tree_cov", "rain", "temp"), type = "response") |>

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: The log link bends a line into a curve
text:
The log link bends a line into a curve

tibble(log_count = seq(-2, 6, length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(count = exp(log_count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log_count, y = count)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "log scale (what the coefficient describes)", y = "count scale (what we care about)")




The log link bends a straight line into an exponential curve.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Computing the rate ratio

exp(fixef(mod_2)$cond["tree_cov"])  # rate ratio: ~2.08, i.e. a ~108% increase per unit tree cover

tree_cov 
1.976689 


Both describe the same underlying model — pick the one that matches your audience (percent change vs. a concrete headcount).

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: Case study: occurrence and abundance together
text:
Case study: occurrence and abundance together
In reality, a species first has to be present before we can measure its abundance. A hurdle model combines two sub-models fit jointly:

A binomial (logit-link) component: does a plot clear the “hurdle” of zero? (occurrence)
A truncated count component: given it’s non-zero, how many individuals? (abundance when present)

Two ways to interpret: each part separately (what drives occurrence vs. abundance), or combined on the population scale (expected abundance across all plots = P(occurrence) × E[abundance | present]).

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
A simple hurdle example

# Simple hurdle simulation: abundance_pres = counts if present; occurence = presence;
# abundance_pop = observed count in every plot (zero wherever the species is absent)
simple_pop_data <- tibble(
  tree_cov = generate(tree_cover, n_plots)
) |>
  unnest(everything()) |>
  mutate(abundance_pres = rpois(n_plots, lambda =
                     abundance_intercept +
                     abundance_tree_effect * tree_cov
                     ),
         occurence = rbinom(n_plots, size = 1,
                     prob = occurence_intercept +
                            occurence_tree_effect * tree_cov),
         abundance_pop = abundance_pres * occurence)

# Hurdle model: main formula is the (zero-truncated Poisson) abundance-when-present part;
# zi = ~ tree_cov models the probability of a structural zero (absence) with a logit link
mod_hu_simple <- glmmTMB(abundance_pop ~ tree_cov,
                         zi = ~ tree_cov,
                         family = truncated_poisson,
                         data = simple_pop_data)

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Population vs. present-only predictions

# type = "response": population-scale expected abundance across ALL plots (P(present) x count)
pred_resp_simple <- predictions(mod_hu_simple, type = "response") |> mutate(type = "response")

# type = "zprob": predicted probability of a structural zero (i.e. NOT occurring)
pred_prob_simple <- predictions(mod_hu_simple, type = "zprob")

# type = "conditional": expected abundance given the species is present
pred_cond_simple <- predictions(mod_hu_simple, type = "conditional") |> mutate(type = "conditional")

pred_abun_simple <- bind_rows(pred_resp_simple, pred_cond_simple)

plot_pred_abun_simple <- ggplot(pred_abun_simple) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = tree_cov, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = type), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = tree_cov, y = estimate, color = type)) +
  labs(x = "Tree cover", y = "Abundance", color = "Prediction type", fill = "Prediction type")

# zprob is P(structural zero), so 1 - zprob is the occurrence probability
plot_pred_prob_simple <- ggplot(pred_prob_simple) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = tree_cov, ymin = 1 - conf.high, ymax = 1 - conf.low), fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(x = tree_cov, y = 1 - estimate)) +
  labs(x = "Tree cover", y = "Occurence probability")

plot_pred_abun_simple / plot_pred_prob_simple




Top: predicted abundance, population-scale (response) vs. when present (conditional). Bottom: predicted occurrence probability (1 - zprob).




Predicted abundance when present (conditional) is always higher than population-scale abundance (response), since occurrence probability is below 100%. This is an implicit interaction between the model’s two parts: tree cover’s effect on population-scale abundance depends on its effect on both occurrence and abundance-when-present.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Simulating with an explicit interaction
Prey and competitors interact in their effect on abundance (when present); tree cover drives occurrence only. Predictors are simulated through the model’s own inverse link (exp(), plogis()) so they stay in a valid range.

more_plots <- 4000
prey_abun <- dist_poisson(lambda = 6)
competitor_abun <- dist_poisson(lambda = 3)

pop_data <- tibble(
  tree_cov = generate(tree_cover, more_plots),
  prey = generate(prey_abun, more_plots),
  competitors = generate(competitor_abun, more_plots)
) |>
  unnest(everything()) |>
  mutate(
    abundance_pres = rpois(more_plots,
      lambda = exp(1 + 0.12 * prey - 0.15 * competitors - 0.045 * prey * competitors)),
    occurence = rbinom(more_plots, size = 1, prob = plogis(-2 + 0.45 * tree_cov)),
    abundance_pop = abundance_pres * occurence
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(tree_cov, prey, competitors), ~ (.x - mean(.x)) / sd(.x), .names = "scl_{.col}"))

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Fitting the hurdle model

mod_hu <- glmmTMB(
  abundance_pop ~ scl_prey * scl_competitors,
  zi = ~ scl_tree_cov,
  family = truncated_poisson,
  data = pop_data
)

zi = ~ scl_tree_cov: the zero-inflation (occurrence) part. The conditional formula’s scl_prey * scl_competitors is an explicit interaction, layered on top of the log link’s implicit one.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: The interaction on the count scale
text:
The interaction on the count scale

slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey",
       newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors),
                                                 max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30)),
       type = "response") |>
  # unscale back to raw competitor counts for an interpretable x-axis
  mutate(competitors = scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line() +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(count scale, individuals present)", x = "Competitors",
       title = "Count-scale effect of prey availability weakens as competitors increase")




Count-scale effect of prey weakens (and reverses) as competitors increase.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: The interaction on the link scale
text:
The interaction on the link scale

slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey",
       newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors),
                                                 max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30)),
       type = "link") |>
  # unscale back to raw competitor counts for an interpretable x-axis
  mutate(competitors = scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "blue", linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.4, fill = "lightgrey") +
  geom_line() +
  labs(y = "Slope of scl_prey\n(log scale)", x = "Competitors",
       title = "Link-scale effect of prey declines linearly with competitors")




Link-scale effect of prey is a straight, non-zero-crossing line in competitors — the explicit interaction, undistorted by the log link.




Unlike the count-scale plot, this one is linear in competitors by construction — the model’s formula (scl_prey * scl_competitors) is fit additively on the log scale, so the explicit interaction shows up here as a straight line, with no additional curvature from the log link itself.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Isolating the interaction: rate ratios
To isolate something closer to “the interaction itself,” we move to the rate-ratio scale: for each one-SD increase in competitors, by what factor does the effect of one extra SD of prey get multiplied? That’s exp() of the interaction coefficient, and because it lives on the model’s own additive (log) scale, it doesn’t depend on where competitors are evaluated — unlike the count-scale slope.

rate_ratio_interaction_tbl <- avg_slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey",
                                          by = "scl_competitors",
                                          newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = c(-1, 0, 1)),
                                          type = "link") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = exp(estimate), rr_low = exp(conf.low), rr_high = exp(conf.high)) |>
  select(scl_competitors, rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high, p.value) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    p.value = if_else(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(p.value, 3)))
  ) |>
  mutate(CI_95 = glue::glue("[{rr_low}, {rr_high}]")) |>
  select(`Competitors (scaled)` = scl_competitors, `Rate ratio for scl_prey` = rate_ratio, `95% CI` = CI_95, `p-value` = p.value)

rate_ratio_interaction_tbl |>
  tt(caption = "Rate ratio of scl_prey's effect on abundance, evaluated at three levels of scl_competitors")



    

    

    
    
    
      
        Rate ratio of scl_prey's effect on abundance, evaluated at three levels of scl_competitors
        
              
                Competitors (scaled)
                Rate ratio for scl_prey
                95% CI
                p-value
              
        
        
        
                
                  -1
                  1.194
                  [1.111, 1.283]
                  <0.001

Prey’s rate ratio drops from >1 (increasing abundance) at low competitor density to <1 (decreasing abundance) at high competitor density.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Predicted abundance, by competitor level

predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(
    scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
    scl_competitors = fivenum
  ),
  type = "conditional"
) |>
  mutate(prey = scl_prey * sd(pop_data$prey) + mean(pop_data$prey),
         competitors = round(scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors), 1)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = as.factor(competitors)), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate, color = as.factor(competitors))) +
  labs(y = "Predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Prey", color = "Competitors", fill = "Competitors")




Abundance-when-present predictions across prey, one line per competitor five-number-summary level.




At low competitor density, abundance climbs steeply with prey; by the time competitors are abundant, the prey curve is nearly flat — the same shrinking slope we saw before, now shown as predicted trends rather than slopes.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: Population-scale picture: low vs. high tree cover
text:
Population-scale picture: low vs. high tree cover

# Locate the two peaks of tree_cov's bimodal distribution, as scaled values
d <- density(pop_data$tree_cov)
peaks <- d$x[which(diff(sign(diff(d$y))) == -2) + 1]
low_tree_pop <- round(peaks[1], 2)
high_tree_pop <- round(peaks[length(peaks)], 2)
low_tree_pop_scl <- (low_tree_pop - mean(pop_data$tree_cov)) / sd(pop_data$tree_cov)
high_tree_pop_scl <- (high_tree_pop - mean(pop_data$tree_cov)) / sd(pop_data$tree_cov)

predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(
    scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
    scl_competitors = fivenum,
    scl_tree_cov = c(low_tree_pop_scl, high_tree_pop_scl)
  ),
  type = "response"
) |>
  mutate(prey = scl_prey * sd(pop_data$prey) + mean(pop_data$prey),
         competitors = round(scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors), 1),
         `Tree cover` = if_else(scl_tree_cov == low_tree_pop_scl, "Low tree cover", "High tree cover")) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = as.factor(competitors)), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate, color = as.factor(competitors))) +
  facet_wrap(~ `Tree cover`) +
  labs(y = "Predicted population abundance", x = "Prey", color = "Competitors", fill = "Competitors")




Population-scale (response) predictions: prey x competitors, faceted by low vs. high tree cover.




Within each panel, the prey × competitors shape is the same. But the high-tree-cover panel sits above the low-tree-cover panel overall — more plots are occupied there. Tree cover mostly shifts how many plots have the species at all; prey and competitors jointly shape abundance within occupied plots.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: A symmetric interaction, viewed from the other predictor
text:
A symmetric interaction, viewed from the other predictor

predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(
    scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
    scl_prey = fivenum
  ),
  type = "conditional"
) |>
  mutate(competitors = scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors),
         prey = round(scl_prey * sd(pop_data$prey) + mean(pop_data$prey), 1)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = as.factor(prey)), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate, color = as.factor(prey))) +
  labs(y = "Predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Competitors", color = "Prey", fill = "Prey")




Same interaction, axes swapped: competitors on x, one line per prey five-number-summary level.




A two-way interaction is mathematically symmetric: scl_prey:scl_competitors is the same coefficient as scl_competitors:scl_prey. This view makes a different point than the prey-on-x-axis plot: regardless of prey availability, enough competitors drive abundance down to roughly the same low floor. Neither plot is “more correct” — reporting only one risks showing half the story (Spake et al. 2023).

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: Average predictions: one curve per predictor
text:
Average predictions: one curve per predictor

avg_pred_prey_cond <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_prey", type = "conditional"
) |>
  mutate(prey = scl_prey * sd(pop_data$prey) + mean(pop_data$prey))

avg_pred_comp_cond <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = "scl_competitors", type = "conditional"
) |>
  mutate(competitors = scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors))

p_avg_prey_cond <- avg_pred_prey_cond |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = prey, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(x = prey, y = estimate)) +
  labs(y = "Average predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Prey")

p_avg_comp_cond <- avg_pred_comp_cond |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(x = competitors, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate)) +
  labs(y = "Average predicted abundance\n(when present)", x = "Competitors")

p_avg_prey_cond + p_avg_comp_cond




Abundance-when-present, averaged over the full observed range of the other predictor.




datagrid(..., grid_type = "counterfactual") pairs each focal value with every observed row, then averages — a true average over the sample rather than a slope evaluated at the other predictors’ means. Averaged over all observed competitor density, prey still shows a positive effect; averaged over all observed prey, competitors show a diminishing-harm shape.

text:
Population-scale average, by tree cover

avg_pred_prey_resp <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_prey = seq(min(pop_data$scl_prey), max(pop_data$scl_prey), length.out = 30),

                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),

) |>
  mutate(prey = scl_prey * sd(pop_data$prey) + mean(pop_data$prey),
         `Tree cover` = if_else(scl_tree_cov == low_tree_pop_scl, "Low tree cover", "High tree cover"))

avg_pred_comp_resp <- avg_predictions(mod_hu,
  newdata = datagrid(model = mod_hu,
                      scl_competitors = seq(min(pop_data$scl_competitors), max(pop_data$scl_competitors), length.out = 30),
                      scl_tree_cov = c(low_tree_pop_scl, high_tree_pop_scl),
                      grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  by = c("scl_competitors", "scl_tree_cov"), type = "response"
) |>
  mutate(competitors = scl_competitors * sd(pop_data$competitors) + mean(pop_data$competitors),
         `Tree cover` = if_else(scl_tree_cov == low_tree_pop_scl, "Low tree cover", "High tree cover"))

p_avg_prey_resp <- avg_pred_prey_resp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prey, y = estimate, color = `Tree cover`, fill = `Tree cover`)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(y = "Average predicted\npopulation abundance", x = "Prey")

p_avg_comp_resp <- avg_pred_comp_resp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = competitors, y = estimate, color = `Tree cover`, fill = `Tree cover`)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(y = "Average predicted\npopulation abundance", x = "Competitors")

p_avg_prey_resp + p_avg_comp_resp




Population-scale average curves, one pair per tree-cover peak.




The shapes barely change between tree-cover panels — the prey × competitors interaction lives entirely in the abundance-when-present part. What changes is the overall height: high-tree-cover populations sit consistently above low-tree-cover ones, a pure occupancy effect, cleanly separated from the abundance-when-present shape.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
section: A full rate-ratio table, by model component
text:
A full rate-ratio table, by model component

# Conditional-model rate ratio for scl_prey, at three levels of scl_competitors
prey_rr_tbl <- avg_slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_prey", by = "scl_competitors",
                           newdata = datagrid(scl_competitors = c(-1, 0, 1)),
                           type = "link") |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = exp(estimate), rr_low = exp(conf.low), rr_high = exp(conf.high),
         Term = glue::glue("scl_prey (at scl_competitors = {scl_competitors} SD)")) |>
  select(Term, rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high, p.value)

# Conditional-model rate ratio for scl_competitors, at three levels of scl_prey
comp_rr_tbl <- avg_slopes(mod_hu, variables = "scl_competitors", by = "scl_prey",
                           newdata = datagrid(scl_prey = c(-1, 0, 1)),
                           type = "link") |>
  mutate(rate_ratio = exp(estimate), rr_low = exp(conf.low), rr_high = exp(conf.high),
         Term = glue::glue("scl_competitors (at scl_prey = {scl_prey} SD)")) |>
  select(Term, rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high, p.value)

# The interaction itself: ratio of rate ratios per 1-SD increase in the moderator
hu_confint <- confint(mod_hu)
hu_coef_cond <- summary(mod_hu)$coefficients$cond
hu_coef_zi <- summary(mod_hu)$coefficients$zi

interaction_rr_tbl <- tibble(
  Term = "scl_prey:scl_competitors (interaction)",
  rate_ratio = exp(hu_coef_cond["scl_prey:scl_competitors", "Estimate"]),
  rr_low = exp(hu_confint["cond.scl_prey:scl_competitors", "2.5 %"]),
  rr_high = exp(hu_confint["cond.scl_prey:scl_competitors", "97.5 %"]),
  p.value = hu_coef_cond["scl_prey:scl_competitors", "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

# Zero-inflation-model odds ratio for scl_tree_cov (no moderator in this model)
zi_rr_tbl <- tibble(
  Term = "scl_tree_cov (zero-inflation)",
  rate_ratio = exp(hu_coef_zi["scl_tree_cov", "Estimate"]),
  rr_low = exp(hu_confint["zi.scl_tree_cov", "2.5 %"]),
  rr_high = exp(hu_confint["zi.scl_tree_cov", "97.5 %"]),
  p.value = hu_coef_zi["scl_tree_cov", "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

hu_rr_tbl <- bind_rows(
  prey_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Conditional (abundance, when present)"),
  comp_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Conditional (abundance, when present)"),
  interaction_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Conditional (abundance, when present)"),
  zi_rr_tbl |> mutate(Component = "Zero-inflation (occupancy, as an odds ratio)")
) |>
  relocate(Component) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(rate_ratio, rr_low, rr_high), ~ round(.x, 3)),
    p.value = if_else(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(p.value, 3))),
    CI_95 = glue::glue("[{rr_low}, {rr_high}]")
  ) |>
  select(Component, Term, `Rate/odds ratio` = rate_ratio, `95% CI` = CI_95, `p-value` = p.value)

hu_rr_tbl |>
  tt(caption = "Standardized rate ratios (conditional model) and odds ratio (zero-inflation model) for mod_hu") |>
  style_tt(i = which(hu_rr_tbl$Component != dplyr::lag(hu_rr_tbl$Component, default = "")) - 1,
           j = 1:5, line = "b", line_color = "black", line_width = 0.05)

Tree cover’s odds ratio in the zero-inflation part tells a simpler, interaction-free story about occupancy alone.

title: Interactions in Regression Models — Student Handout
text:
Part 3 takeaways

Non-linear link functions (logit, log) create an implicit interaction: every predictor’s response-scale effect depends on the values of all other predictors, even with no interaction term in the formula
Raw GLM coefficients live on the link scale; marginaleffects::slopes() converts them to the natural (probability, count) scale for you
Multiplicative summaries (rate ratios, odds ratios) stay constant across the range of other predictors; additive, response-scale summaries do not
Whether an interaction “exists” can depend on the scale you’re measuring on (Spake et al. 2023) — this applies just as much to implicit link-function interactions as to explicit interaction terms
Hurdle/zero-inflated models separate “does it occur” from “how much, given it occurs” — interpret each part separately, or combine them (type = "response") for a population-scale answer
Interactions are mathematically symmetric: report (or at least check) both “A moderated by B” and “B moderated by A”
